questions.q: If the resistivity of pure silicon is $3000Ωm$ and the mobilities of electrons and holes are $0. 12m^{2}V^{- 1}s^{- 1}$ and $0. 045m^{2}V^{- 1}s^{- 1}$ respectively, then what will be the resistivity of a specimen of silicon when ${10}^{19}$ atoms of phosphorous are added per cubic metre?
questions.solution:
The resistivity of pure $S$ is given by

$ρ = \dfrac{1}{σ} = \dfrac{1}{e\left({n}_{e}{μ}_{e} + {n}_{h}{μ}_{h}\right)} = \dfrac{1}{{en}_{1}\left({μ}_{e} + {μ}_{h}\right)}$

or ${n}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{eρ\left({μ}_{e} + {μ}_{n}\right)} = \dfrac{1}{1. 6 \times {10}^{- 19} \times 3000 ( 0. 12 + 0. 045 )}$

$= 1. 26 \times {10}^{16}m^{- 3}$

When ${10}^{19}$ atoms of phosphorous (donor atoms of valence five) are added per $m^{3},$ the semiconductor becomes $n$ - type semiconductor.

$∴ {n}_{e} - {n}_{h} \approx {n}_{e} = {N}_{d} = {10}^{19} ∵ {n}_{n} = 1. 26 \times {10}^{16}$

Resitivity $ρ = \dfrac{1}{{n}_{e}{μ}_{e}e} = \dfrac{1}{1. 6 \times {10}^{- 19} \times {10}^{19} \times 0. 12} = 5. 21Ωm$

questions.q: The current gain in the common emitter amplifier mode of a transistor is $10$. The input impedance is $20kΩ$ and load resistance is $100kΩ$. The power gain is
questions.solution:
The power gain is defined as the ratio of change in output power and the change in input power.
Since, $P = VI$.


Therefore, Power gain = Current gain X Voltage gain
$= \beta \times \beta \left(\dfrac{Rout}{Rin}\right) = {\beta}^{2}\left(\dfrac{Rout}{Rin}\right)


Given, \beta =$10$, ${R}_{in} = 20kΩ and {R}_{out} = 100kΩ$.
Hence, Power gain $= {$\left(10\right)$}^{2}$\left(\dfrac{100}{20}\right) =$100 \times$5 = 500$

questions.solution:

questions.solution: Here, the emitter-base junction of the N-P-N transistor is forward biased with battery ${V}_{BB}$ through resistance $R$. When the value of $R$ is reduced, then the base current ${i}_{b}$ will increase. As a result, the collector current will also increase. $( {i}_{c} = \beta{i}_{b} )$. Due to the increase in ${i}_{c}$, the potential difference across $L$ increases and hence the reading of voltmeter will increase.

questions.q:
In a common emitter transistor amplifier, signal voltage across the collector resistance of $2kΩ$ is $2volt$. What should be the value of resistance ${R}_{B}$ in series with ${V}_{BB}$ voltage supply of $2volt$ in the input circuit, if the $D. C.$ base current is $10$times the signal current in ${R}_{B}$?

$(Given: base emitter voltage ${V}_{BE} = 0.6V$, current amplification factor ${β}_{ac} \approx {β}_{dc} = 100)
questions.solution:
$\left({i}_{c}\right)AC = \dfrac{\left({V}_{out }\right)AC}{RC} = \dfrac{2\text{volt}}{2kΩ} = 1mA$

$\left({i}_{B}\right)AC = \dfrac{\left({i}_{c}\right)AC}{\betaac} = \dfrac{1mA}{100} = 0 . 01mA$

$\left({i}_{B}\right)DC = 10\left({i}_{B}\right)AC = 0 . 1mA = {10}^{- 4}A$

${R}_{B} = \dfrac{V}{iB} = \dfrac{2 - 0 . 6}{10- 4} = 14kΩ$

questions.q: The transfer characteristic curve of a transistor, having input and output resistance $100Ω$ and $100kΩ$ respectively, is shown in the figure. The voltage and power gain, are respectively:
questions.solution:
Current gain $\left(\beta\right) = \dfrac{\Delta{I}_{C}}{\Delta{I}_{B}} = \dfrac{5 \times {10}^{- 3}}{100 \times {10}^{- 6}} = 50$
Voltage gain $( {\text{A}}_{\text{V}} ) = \beta\left(\dfrac{{R}_{out}}{{R}_{in}}\right) = 50 \times \dfrac{100 \times {10}^{3}}{100} = 5 \times {10}^{4}$
Power gain $= {A}_{V} \times \beta = 50 \times 5 \times {10}^{4} = 2.5 \times {10}^{6}$

questions.q:
A $CE$ amplifier, has a power gain of $40dB$ . The input resistance and output load resistance are $500Ω$ and $2\text{k}Ω$ respectively. Find the value of common-emitter current gain.
[Take gain in $dB = 10log\left(\dfrac{{P}_{out}}{{P}_{in}}\right)$]
questions.solution:
Given that,
Power gain $( {A}_{\text{P}} ) = 40\text{dB}$
$∴ 10log\left(\dfrac{{P}_{0}}{{P}_{in}}\right) = 40$
$∴ log\left(\dfrac{{P}_{0}}{{P}_{m}}\right) = 4$
$∴ \dfrac{{P}_{0}}{{P}_{\text{in}}} = {10}^{4}$
Also, ${A}_{\text{P}} = {\beta}^{2} \times$ Resistance gain
$= {\beta}^{2} \times \left(\dfrac{{R}_{out}}{{R}_{in}}\right)$
$= {\beta}^{2} \times \dfrac{2000}{500}$
$= {\beta}^{2} \times 4$
$∴ {\beta}^{2} = \dfrac{{10}^{4}}{4}$
$∴ \beta = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50$

questions.q: A change of $8. 0mA$ in the emitter current brings a change of $7. 9mA$ in the collector current. The values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are
questions.solution:
Given that, change in emitter current, $∆ {I}_{E} = 8mA$ and change in collector current, $∆ {I}_{C} = 7.9mA$.
We know that,
$\alpha = \dfrac{{∆ I}_{C}}{{∆ I}_{E}}$
$⇒ \alpha = \dfrac{7.9}{8}$
$⇒ \alpha \approx 0. 99$
Also, we know that
$\beta = \dfrac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}$
$⇒ \beta = \dfrac{\dfrac{7.9}{8}}{1 - \dfrac{7.9}{8}} = \dfrac{7.9}{8 - 7.9}$
$⇒ \beta = \dfrac{7.9}{0.1} = 79$
Hence, the required answer is $\alpha = 0. 99$ and $\beta = 79$.

questions.q: A common emitter amplifier has a voltage gain of 50, an input impedance of 100 $Ω$ and an output impedance of 200 $Ω.$ The power gain of the amplifier is
questions.solution:
AC power gain = $\dfrac{Changeinoutputpower}{Changeininputpower}$

= $\dfrac{{∆ V}_{c} × {∆ i}_{c}}{{∆ V}_{i} × {∆ i}_{b}} = \left(\dfrac{{∆ V}_{c}}{{∆ V}_{i}}\right) × \left(\dfrac{{∆ i}_{c}}{{∆ i}_{b}}\right) = {A}_{V} × {β}_{AC}$

where ${A}_{V}isvoltagegain$ and ${\left(β\right)}_{AC}$ is AC current gain.

Also,

${A}_{V} = {β}_{AC} × resistancegain \left(= \dfrac{{R}_{o}}{{R}_{i}}\right)

Given, ${A}_{V} = 50, {R}_{o} = 200Ω, {R}_{i} = 100Ω$

Hence, 50 = ${β}_{AC} × $\dfrac{200}{100}

$∴{β}_{AC} = 25$

Now, AC power gain = ${A}_{V} × {β}_{AC}$ = 50 $×$ 25 = 1250$

$\to \dfrac{3 / 4}{1 / 4} = \dfrac{{n}_{e}}{{n}_{h}} × \dfrac{5}{2}$

$\to \dfrac{{n}_{e}}{{n}_{h}} = \dfrac{6}{5}$
